Hi, fuckyeahgoats. I started gardening again this year for the first time since my teens. Lets start with some basics:

  1. What zone are you in?

  2. How much space is not lots? How much depth in terms of soil can you get?

  3. How much light does your garden plot get?

  4. Besides attracting bees, do you have any goals in mind?

I have some big pine trees that shade the area I would be putting the garden in, but it still gets a good amount of light. Soil depth, I'm not sure on but I was planning on garden boxes. How do I go about this?

Okay, we can work with this! Without a doubt, I say go for constructing the raised beds and filling them with a good 3-in-1 soil mix (black earth, rotted manure and coconut husk fiber - available at most garden outlets.) If you want to do potatoes, you could build smaller, albeit taller raised beds so that they have plenty of room to fill out. I've found that raised beds are easier to work in and aren't as prone to going wild with weeds. Depending on the design, they can also be helpful in keeping animals out.

The vegetables you've mentioned should do quite well in this configuration, but I would suggest keeping things like tomatoes and peppers in as much light as possible. You should also make sure you clear any pine needle debris and try to keep the soil pH between 6 - 6.5 for best results. It varies, but everything generally produces around 6.5. Cucumbers, peas and certain varieties of squash like to climb, so prepare to add trellising shortly after your seedlings break through.

Consider your pairings (pdf warning) as well. Onions make great sentinels for things like carrots to keep the pests away. If you want smaller and more flavorful carrots, plant them along with your tomatoes, leaving enough room for the adult plant. I planted my tomatoes a few beds away from my potatoes, as both are of the Nightshade family and can share diease. It also never hurts to add some colour to your garden, like marigolds. If you can tolerate the smell, they also help in keeping pests away.

This growing season has been especially wet for me, so I sort of made raised beds in my raised bed. I've found that it helps with drainage, ymmv.

Oh, neat. Zone eleven? You're fortunate as far as choices go - you can do thing that I wouldn't dare. At this point in the season, you're likely going to want to buy up some already started crops. The sense that I'm getting here is that you should really start small. If you're handy with tools, construct yourself a raised bed or two. If not, consider creating standard rows somewhere between 40-45cm wide with about 90cm between as a walkway. This is important if you intend to plant crops like potatoes, as the standard method involves hoeing up the beds a few times as they break through - it is often referred to as mounding.

If you'd like to start smaller, you can always hunt around thrift shops - as they often tend to have planters on the cheap. You can grow several crops in planters with varying degrees of success. For your climate, you can do things like Cillantro, Chives, Basil, Lemon Grass, Mexican Tarragon and Oregano for spices. Rosemary's great for fish and poultry as well, so why not.

If you'd really like to take good advantage of your climate and sun conditions, I'd say try peppers and cantaloupes. You can pair your peppers with chives and onions to deter pests, and the basil as an (alleged) flavor boost. As for the cantaloupe, tansy, marigold and dill seem to get on well - but ensure that you've taken spacing and vining. You can trellis train your cantaloupe so that it doesn't kill the ground cover you've paired with it to ward off pests.

The Investment Chapter highlights the intent of the TPP negotiating parties, led by the United States, to increase the power of global corporations by creating a supra-national court, or tribunal, where foreign firms can "sue" states and obtain taxpayer compensation for "expected future profits". These investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) tribunals are designed to overrule the national court systems. ISDS tribunals introduce a mechanism by which multinational corporations can force governments to pay compensation if the tribunal states that a country's laws or policies affect the company's claimed future profits. In return, states hope that multinationals will invest more. Similar mechanisms have already been used. For example, US tobacco company Phillip Morris used one such tribunal to sue Australia (June 2011 – ongoing) for mandating plain packaging of tobacco products on public health grounds; and by the oil giant Chevron against Ecuador in an attempt to evade a multi-billion-dollar compensation ruling for polluting the environment. The threat of future lawsuits chilled environmental and other legislation in Canada after it was sued by pesticide companies in 2008/9. ISDS tribunals are often held in secret, have no appeal mechanism, do not subordinate themselves to human rights laws or the public interest, and have few means by which other affected parties can make representations.
